headline: Mostly dry now; thunderstorms may affect southwest England later.
summary:
The latest MSLP charts show weak high pressure centred close to western Scotland, with a slack pressure pattern across England and Wales. Compared with Wednesday evening, the ridge has edged west and pressure has risen slightly, leaving no organised frontal system over England and Wales while Atlantic rain remains well to the west of Ireland.

Observed rainfall in the last 24 hours has been light, with the highest gauge total 7.0mm at Bethesda Quarry in northwest Wales, followed by 2.7mm at Kinsford Gate in southwest England and 2.5mm at Brotherswater in Cumbria. Daily accumulation maps show earlier wetter spells across parts of southeast and central southern England on Monday and Tuesday, but little meaningful antecedent rainfall over England and Wales in the past 24 hours; active Met Office warnings are for extreme heat widely and a Yellow thunderstorm warning for South West England this evening, with no named storm.

UKV (run Thu 25/0400 BST) gives the largest day-1 area-mean totals in South West England at 5.2mm up to early Friday morning (Fri 26/0400 BST), with county maxima of 17.1mm in South Gloucestershire, 14.3mm in Bath and North East Somerset and 10.8mm in Bristol; Wales reaches 1.3mm and the West Midlands 3.0mm over the same period. For day 2, UKV (run Thu 25/0400 BST) shifts the wettest England and Wales area-means to northeast England with 1.8mm up to early Saturday morning (Sat 27/0400 BST), including 5.4mm across Stockton-on-Tees and 5.2mm in Tyne and Wear, so flood risk remains generally VERY LOW overall with local LOW surface water risk possible in parts of southwest England later today and on Friday.

Respond with a JSON object inside <json> tags:
- "headline": One sentence, max 12 words.
- "summary": Three paragraphs separated by \n\n. Two sentences each — be direct and concise. MANDATORY structure, never merge:
    Para 1 — Synoptic scene: describe what the MSLP charts show and how the pattern has changed; name the feature driving the weather (front, low, ridge etc).
    Para 2 — Recent observations: where the heaviest rain fell in the last 24h with gauge point-totals and region names; note antecedent context from the daily accumulation maps and any active Met Office warnings (naming any storm).
    Para 3 — Outlook: UKV day-1 and day-2 area-mean totals for the wettest regions and catchments, cited as "UKV (run ddd D/HHMM BST/GMT)" with natural valid-time phrases like "up to early Friday morning (Fri 25/0300 BST)"; close with a brief flood-risk conclusion referencing FGS levels (block caps: VERY LOW, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH) only if relevant.

Rainfall thresholds: 10mm/1h heavy; 30mm/1h extreme; 100mm/24h exceptional.

Style: professional third-person prose; no bullet points; specific place names and mm values. Gauge values are single-site point totals; UKV values are spatial area-means — keep these distinct. All times in GMT or BST — never UTC. Use natural time phrases where possible (e.g. "compared with yesterday morning", "up to early Friday"); you may bracket the precise time for verifiability. Only mention meteorological mechanisms (orographic enhancement, frontal lifting, convective instability, etc.) where the radar imagery, gauge distribution, or MSLP charts specifically support it — do not assert mechanisms without evidence. Say flood risk once, proportionately, at the end. In quiet conditions say so plainly.
